title: Zero new dies for 24 months: robotic chip-level DIMM reclamation
idea: Self-imposed limit: no fresh dies allowed. Robotic lines desolder DRAM packages from retired hyperscaler DIMMs, reball, retest and speed-bin each die, then remount them on CXL Type-3 expanders whose controller trains per-die timing so mixed-speed reclaimed DDR4/DDR5 dies run as one pool.
why: Supply/reuse: retired fleets discard tens of millions of working GB a year; recovering 30-50% of it adds several percent to usable bit supply at ~$1/GB rework cost with zero wafer starts.

title: Every failed die must ship: salvage-grade DRAM with controller sparing
idea: Self-imposed limit: no die is scrapped. Fabs sell dies that fail speed or have more bad rows than fuse repair covers as a 'salvage grade'; a host or CXL controller with large row-remap tables and spare-die striping uses them for KV-cache and cold tiers that tolerate lower speed.
why: Recovers part of the 10-20% wafer yield fallout as usable bits; +3-8% effective supply with no new capex.

title: Buyers with zero capex budget: cooperative prepaid DRAM capacity bonds
idea: Self-imposed limit: mid-tier buyers cannot fund fabs on their balance sheets. A buyers' cooperative issues prepaid capacity bonds that finance a dedicated line at an existing maker under take-or-pay; each member's bond share sets its allocation priority in shortages.
why: Capital intensity and allocation: turns fragmented demand into financeable offtake for a $3-5B line; members get shortage-proof allocation instead of 4x spot.

title: No fab below 15 nm: U.S. legacy-DRAM relief line on licensed IP
idea: Self-imposed limit: only mature nodes. License DDR3/DDR4/LPDDR4 designs and process recipes from makers exiting legacy DRAM and run them in a U.S. 2x-nm line for automotive, industrial and networking buyers, so leading makers can move those wafers to HBM and DDR5.
why: U.S. manufacturability and supply: legacy bits are roughly 10-15% of demand. A depreciated, DUV-only process gives on-shore supply in 2-3 years at a fraction of leading-edge capex.

title: No server may own its RAM: spot market per GB-second
idea: Self-imposed limit: memory is only rented. A CXL-switched rack pool runs an internal exchange where VMs bid for capacity by the GB-second. Stranded memory, which is 25-50% of provisioned DRAM in clouds, is auctioned back within milliseconds via page migration.
why: Do the job with less: cuts the DRAM provisioned per server by 10-25% fleet-wide through price signals rather than static sizing.

title: Each GB serves three owners: content-addressed shared weight memory
idea: Self-imposed limit: every byte must have at least three readers. Model weights are hashed and stored once in a read-only CXL shared-memory segment that dozens of inference hosts map at the same time, instead of each host keeping its own copy in local DRAM.
why: Host DRAM in inference fleets is dominated by duplicate weights; deduplication cuts that footprint 3-10x.

title: No proprietary IP: open DRAM design kit for trench foundries
idea: Self-imposed limit: everything must be open. A consortium releases an open-licensed DRAM macro kit (trench or stacked cell, sense amp, redundancy, DDR/CXL PHY RTL) qualified on foundry processes that already have deep-trench capacitors, so any logic foundry can make commodity-interface DRAM.
why: Breaks the three-maker oligopoly and the IP barrier; adds foundry capacity to DRAM supply. Density is lower, but U.S. manufacturability improves.

title: Helium at zero for a year: recapture-and-substitute retrofit leasing
idea: Self-imposed limit: no helium deliveries. Leased retrofit kits recover helium from etch-chuck backside cooling and load-locks with membrane and cryogenic recovery (>90%), and switch tolerant chucks to hydrogen or argon backside gas. They are priced per wafer, not as capex.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: keeps fabs running through the Qatar helium outage (about 30% of supply) and cuts helium per wafer by about 10x.

title: Spruce Pine cut off: synthetic-silica crucible liners from polysilicon byproduct
idea: Self-imposed limit: no natural high-purity quartz. Crucible inner layers are made from sol-gel synthetic silica derived from SiCl4, a waste stream of polysilicon plants, and CZ pullers run multi-recharge pulls so each crucible yields 3-5 ingots.
why: Removes the Spruce Pine chokepoint (>80%) for CZ wafers and cuts crucibles per wafer by 3-5x.

title: Tungsten embargo: WF6 exhaust recapture and closed-loop W recovery
idea: Self-imposed limit: no new tungsten imports. Cold-trap and sorbent modules on W-CVD exhaust capture unreacted WF6 for re-fluorination, and spent targets and chamber kits go to a hydrometallurgical W recovery loop at the fab.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: cuts virgin tungsten per wafer by about 50% or more and reduces exposure to the roughly 80% China supply share.

title: No private stockpiles: Strategic DRAM Reserve buying known-good die
idea: Self-imposed limit: only the state may hoard. A federal reserve buys wafers and known-good dies during price troughs, stores them under nitrogen, and releases them in spikes under a price-trigger rule, as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve does.
why: Damps the 4x price swings and gives makers a buyer of last resort in downturns, which supports steady capex.

title: Downturns may not kill capex: revenue-floor insurance for builders
idea: Self-imposed limit: no fab plan may be cancelled because of the cycle. A government-backed insurer guarantees a per-bit revenue floor to makers who keep building through troughs, funded by premiums and clawbacks at peak prices.
why: Capital intensity: removes the cyclical underinvestment behind today's shortage and keeps 3-5-year fab timelines from restarting.

title: Tester hours halved: finish DRAM characterization in the deployed server
idea: Self-imposed limit: half the ATE and burn-in hours. Parts ship after a shortened screen; in-DIMM BIST plus post-package repair finish margin and retention characterization during the first week in a server, and the fleet telemetry feeds back to the fab.
why: Test capital and throughput: test/burn-in capacity effectively doubles, removing a back-end bottleneck to bit output.

title: No HBM stack scrapped: base-die remap into lower-capacity SKUs
idea: Self-imposed limit: zero stack scrap. Stacks with one or two dead core dies are remapped by base-die logic into 6- or 10-high equivalent SKUs, with channels re-striped, and sold to inference customers who need bandwidth more than capacity.
why: HBM yield is down 20-30%; salvaging half of the failed stacks recovers 10-15% of HBM output.

title: Only used tools: U.S. depot rebuilding turnkey DRAM fab kits
idea: Self-imposed limit: no new tool purchases. A U.S. depot buys retired 2x/1x-nm DRAM tool sets from Asian lines, rebuilds them to spec with new controls, and sells them as qualified, matched 'fab kits' with process recipes.
why: Capital and time: cuts tool capex by 60-80% and lead time from years to months for mature-node DRAM capacity.

title: Own zero EUV: tolling critical layers at a partner scanner
idea: Self-imposed limit: no EUV ownership. A DUV-only DRAM fab ships sealed, nitrogen-purged FOUPs to a partner's EUV cell for only the 1-2 layers where multipatterning is uneconomic, paying per exposure.
why: Capital intensity: avoids $200M+ per scanner and its single-supplier queue while keeping 1b-class density.

title: Every byte must be borrowed: off-peak HBM lending over scale-up fabric
idea: Self-imposed limit: no new memory for batch jobs. The cluster scheduler lends idle HBM on lightly loaded inference GPUs at night as remote memory over NVLink-class fabric for training checkpoints and KV spill.
why: Raises HBM utilization from diurnal lows of about 30-40%, which avoids buying extra capacity.

title: Buyer carries the inventory: DRAM wafer tolling contracts
idea: Self-imposed limit: the fab owns no product risk. A hyperscaler buys raw wafers, chemicals and masks, owns the work-in-process, and pays the fab a fixed conversion fee per wafer, the way oil refineries are paid under tolling contracts.
why: Capital intensity: moves price risk and working capital off the maker, making new lines financeable at lower cost of capital.

title: Imports cost 2x: back-end-first U.S. onshoring ladder
idea: Self-imposed limit: tariffs double the cost of finished imports. Import wafers, and run die sort, stacking, TSV reveal and HBM assembly in the U.S. first. Each step funds the next until the front end follows.
why: U.S. manufacturability: builds onshore share from 1-2% upward in rungs that each take 2-3 years and less than $2B.

title: Every GB sold must come back: DRAM module deposit-refund
idea: Self-imposed limit: no DRAM leaves the loop. A per-GB deposit at sale is refunded when modules are returned to certified reclaimers, which guarantees feedstock for die harvesting and cascade reuse.
why: Reuse supply: return rates rise from under 20% to over 80%, turning e-waste into a steady secondary bit supply.

title: Capacity frozen: retrofit CXL compression expanders for cold pages
idea: Self-imposed limit: no new DRAM bits at all. A drop-in CXL card with line-rate LZ/ZSTD-class hardware compresses cold pages, so each physical GB serves 2-3 logical GB with hot pages left uncompressed.
why: Do the job with less: 1.5-2.5x effective capacity on the memory-bound tier.

title: Each new fab under $1B: replicated fab-in-a-box pods
idea: Self-imposed limit: a capex cap of $1B. Standardize a 5k-wafer-start-per-month DRAM cleanroom pod with a fixed tool set, prefabricated utilities and a copy-exact recipe, then replicate pods side by side as demand grows.
why: Capital intensity and time: smaller increments cut financing risk and time to first bits (about 18 months), replacing $15B bets.

title: Users must hedge the cycle: cash-settled DRAM bit futures
idea: Self-imposed limit: no unhedged exposure. An exchange lists a standardized cash-settled future per Gb of DDR5-equivalent, so buyers lock in prices and makers sell output forward to finance capex years ahead.
why: Capital intensity: forward sales lower the cost of capital and smooth the price spikes that starve investment.

title: No silicon wafer: idle Gen 8.5 LCD fabs make oxide-TFT memory panels
idea: Forced limit: no Si wafers. Convert overbuilt Gen 8.5 LCD backplane fabs (2.2x2.5 m glass, about 70x the area of a 300 mm wafer) to make IGZO 2T gain-cell arrays at about 1 um rules, sold as a slow-DRAM capacity tier.
why: Capital and supply: reuses stranded display capacity worth tens of billions; about 30 GB per panel per tier, near parity at shortage prices for a capacity tier.

title: No wafer at all: roll-to-roll steel-foil memory with drum nanoimprint
idea: Forced limit: no discrete substrates. Stainless-steel foil gets a planarizing dielectric, then sputtered oxide-semiconductor and drum-nanoimprinted gain-cell layers in a continuous web line.
why: Capital intensity: web processing cuts tool cost per m2 by about 10x versus batch wafers; foil is cheap and plentiful.

title: No silicon wafer: idle SiC power fabs build refresh-free retention memory
idea: Forced limit: the substrate must not be Si. Overbuilt 200 mm SiC fabs, idle after the EV slowdown, make 1T1C cells whose 3.3 eV-bandgap access transistors leak orders of magnitude less than Si, giving refresh intervals of minutes to hours for standby tiers.
why: Removes refresh energy (46 fJ/bit, 16-33% of idle power) for standby tiers and uses stranded SiC capacity. Density is modest.

title: No silicon: GaN-on-sapphire periphery from idle LED fabs
idea: Forced limit: no Si wafer for CMOS periphery. Idle LED MOCVD fabs grow AlGaN/GaN HEMT sense-amp and driver dies on sapphire (2DEG mobility about 1500 cm2/Vs), which are flip-bonded along the edges of glass oxide-TFT memory arrays.
why: Periphery is 49% of the die; putting it on fast GaN from stranded LED capacity lets cheap glass arrays reach about 50 ns access.

title: No silicon wafer: memory built inside glass-core package substrates
idea: Forced limit: no memory die. Substrate makers deposit oxide-TFT gain-cell tiers directly on the glass core of advanced package substrates (about 510x515 mm panels), so the substrate under the processor is itself a near-memory tier.
why: Supply and data movement: package-substrate makers become memory makers, and the wire to the processor is millimetres long, cutting I/O energy toward 1 pJ/bit.

title: No silicon wafer: phone display backplane doubles as standby memory
idea: Forced limit: the memory must ride on an existing non-Si substrate. Low-leakage oxide TFTs already in LTPO phone backplanes get a few hundred MB of gain-cell array in the bezel and backplane, used as frame buffer and standby memory so the LPDDR can sleep.
why: Supply: about 1.5 billion phones a year could each offload 0.25-0.5 GB of LPDDR demand, which frees wafers for servers.

title: No silicon wafer: 300 mm glass wafers through existing BEOL lines
idea: Forced limit: no CZ silicon. Run oxide-semiconductor memory stacks on 300 mm borosilicate glass wafers in existing BEOL-only tool sets (all steps at or below 400 C). The process needs no crystal pulling, quartz crucibles or FEOL implant and anneal.
why: Removes the Spruce Pine crucible and CZ chokepoints, and substrate cost drops by 5-10x. It uses idle BEOL capacity at mature foundries.

title: No silicon: roll-to-roll MoS2 memory grown on copper foil
idea: Forced limit: the channel and substrate must be non-Si. Monolayer MoS2 is grown by CVD on a continuous copper foil web, transferred to glass or polyimide, and patterned into gain-cell access transistors whose wide bandgap gives sub-fA leakage.
why: Lower leakage reduces refresh, and 2D channels allow scaling without a wafer; supply comes from the copper-foil battery industry.

title: No wafer consumed: remote epitaxy on a reusable donor
idea: Forced limit: the substrate may not be used up. Crystalline Ge or InGaZnO-class films are grown by remote epitaxy through graphene on a donor that is reused 50 or more times, peeled off, and laminated onto glass or metal carriers.
why: Substrate consumption per device drops by about 50x, which decouples memory output from wafer and crucible supply.

title: No silicon wafer: HDD media lines make MRAM crossbars on glass disks
idea: Forced limit: use another industry's substrate and tools. Hard-disk media lines, which sputter thousands of glass platters an hour and nanoimprint bit-patterned media, deposit MTJ plus threshold-selector crossbars on 95 mm glass disks.
why: Capital: reuses a shrinking HDD media industry with world-class sputter and nanoimprint tools, adding non-Si, endurance-unlimited memory capacity.

title: Off-silicon creates an indium chokepoint: switch to indium-free ZTO channels
idea: Forced limit, plus a second one: no Si and no indium. Gain-cell channels use zinc-tin oxide and Ga-free amorphous oxides deposited by ALD, avoiding indium, whose refining is concentrated in China.
why: Scarce resources: keeps a non-Si memory industry from trading the quartz chokepoint for an indium one; Zn and Sn supply is widely distributed.

title: No silicon: mine indium from scrapped LCD panels for oxide memory
idea: Forced limit: indium only from waste. Shred end-of-life LCD panels, leach the ITO with acid, and recover indium by solvent extraction into IGZO targets for oxide-memory lines.
why: Scarce resources: a secondary indium supply equal to a large share of primary output, sourced in the U.S. from e-waste.

title: No Si wafer: relocate retired Gen 6 display toolsets stateside
idea: Forced limit: no Si and no new tools. Buy complete Gen 6 backplane tool sets (PECVD, sputter, panel steppers) from retiring Japanese, Korean and Taiwanese LCD fabs and reinstall them in a U.S. brownfield to make oxide-TFT memory panels.
why: U.S. manufacturability: an onshore memory-substrate line for under $1B in about 2 years, where the U.S. today has almost no display fabs.

title: No silicon wafer: laser-lift-off memory foils laminated onto packages
idea: Forced limit: no thick substrate. Oxide-TFT memory tiers are built on polyimide on a reusable glass carrier, released with flexible-OLED laser lift-off, and laminated as micron-thin memory foils onto logic packages.
why: Uses the large flexible-OLED LLO base. The carrier is reused, and thin foils stack without TSVs, avoiding the HBM TSV tax.

title: No silicon wafer: panel-scale nanoimprint to sub-100 nm rules
idea: Forced limit: glass panels must reach DRAM-like density without EUV. Step-and-repeat nanoimprint templates are pattern-stitched across Gen 6 glass to print sub-100 nm gain-cell features, with die-by-die alignment correcting glass distortion.
why: Density and capital: at 100 nm a Gen 6 panel holds about 1-2 TB, similar to one or two DRAM wafers, with no scanner.

title: No silicon wafer: all-on-glass LTPO memory with LTPS periphery
idea: Forced limit: periphery cannot sit on a Si wafer. Laser-crystallized LTPS CMOS forms decoders and sense amps, and IGZO forms the low-leakage storage cells, all on one glass sheet with the LTPO process phones already use.
why: A complete memory chip with no wafer; reuses LTPO capacity at display makers, and the low-leakage cells allow long refresh intervals.

title: No silicon, no dicing: undiced panel-scale memory slab appliance
idea: Forced limit: the panel is never cut. A whole oxide-TFT memory panel with panel-level redundancy (spare tiles fused out by laser) is laminated into a rack-mounted CXL memory slab with dozens of edge controllers.
why: Removes dicing, packaging and yield loss per die; one slab supplies hundreds of GB of capacity tier at panel cost.

title: No silicon wafer: substrate-neutral CHIPS grants paid per verified bit-capacity
idea: Forced limit: subsidies cannot favour Si. A grant tranche pays per verified Gb of monthly capacity added per dollar of capex, open to glass, foil, SiC and disk lines, with milestones audited by third-party benchmark.
why: Capital: steers public money to the cheapest bits per dollar rather than incumbent process paths.

title: No silicon wafer: federal guaranteed offtake for first non-Si memory
idea: Forced limit: the first buyers must be guaranteed. Federal agencies pre-commit to buy a fixed volume of qualified non-Si memory modules at a set price for five years, as Operation Warp Speed did for vaccines.
why: Removes demand risk that stops investors funding unproven substrates; brings first capacity forward by years.

title: No silicon, no litho: self-ordered anodic alumina capacitor templates
idea: Forced limit: no wafer and no capacitor lithography. Aluminium foil from electrolytic-capacitor plants is anodized into self-ordered nanopores (AR 100+), lined by ALD with high-k and electrodes as storage capacitors, then bonded to TFT access arrays.
why: Capacitor charge wall: AR beyond 115 with no lithography or EUV; reuses the capacitor-foil industry.

title: No silicon wafer: multi-project panel shuttles for memory startups
idea: Forced limit: startups cannot afford a wafer lot. A panel foundry runs shared Gen 6 glass shuttles where 100 or more startups each get a tile of oxide-memory process, at about 1/100 of a mask set and lot.
why: Capital: cuts prototype cost from millions to tens of thousands of dollars and speeds non-Si memory innovation.

title: No silicon, no vacuum: EHD-jet printed oxide memory micro-fabs
idea: Forced limit: no wafer, no vacuum fab. Electrohydrodynamic jet printers write solution-processed ZTO/IGZO and metal lines at about 1 um on glass sheets in $5M micro-fabs distributed near users.
why: Distributed manufacturing: capital per site drops by about 1000x, giving local supply for defense and edge niches; density is low.

title: No silicon wafer: monolithic oxide tiers multiply panel density
idea: Forced limit: panels cannot shrink to DRAM litho. Stack 8-32 monolithic IGZO gain-cell tiers on glass at 350 C or below, each tier self-aligned to the one below with shared staircase contacts.
why: Density: tiers instead of nodes multiply bits per panel by up to 32x, reaching the roughly 26-tier break-even on cheap glass.
